catalog_quote: Gussenhoven 2000 (Roermond): "Within the word, two types of restriction conspire to confine the tonal contrast to certain locations. Firstly, the contrast is restricted to the syllable with main stress. The dialect of Roermond has the same stress system as standard Dutch. Main stress falls on either of the rightmost two syllables of the word if the penult is closed, and on one of the last three rightmost syllables if the penult is open. A final syllable without main word stress can be strong, i.e. form a foot. Secondly, the contrast is restricted to syllables with two sonorant moras. Thus, the syllable rime must contain a long vowel, a diphthong, or a lax vowel followed by a sonorant consonant ... in order for the contrast to exist. As a result, words whose main-stressed syllable contains only a single sonorant mora have neither Accent I nor Accent II." Peters 2006 (Hasselt): "Stress lo…

new_statements.quote: p. 90: “2. De woordklemtoon als drager van het contrast. Het contrast is gelokaliseerd in de lettergreep met woordklemtoon. Samenstellingen hebben overigens (minstens) twee van zulke plaatsen, omdat elk samenstellend woord onafhankelijk een woordaccent bijdraagt. 3. Zinsaccenten. Onafhankelijk van het tooncontrast worden woorden geaccentueerd in de zin, op dezelfde manier als in het Standaardduits en Standaardnederlands.” p. 105: “Hermans (1994) noemt woorden met de klemtoon op de voorvoorlaatste en een secundaire klemtoon op de laatste lettergreep, zoals 1alge1bra, 1domi1nee, die in het Maasbrachts alleen Accent 2 kunnen hebben.”
new_statements.translation: p. 90: “2. Word stress as the carrier of the contrast. The contrast is located in the syllable with word stress. Compounds, incidentally, have (at least) two such positions, because each component word independently contributes a word accent. 3. Sentence accents. Independently of the tone contrast, words are accented in the sentence in the same way as in Standard German and Standard Dutch.” p. 105: “Hermans (1994) mentions words with stress on the antepenultimate and secondary stress on the final syllable, such as 1alge1bra, 1domi1nee, which in the Maasbracht dialect can only have Accent 2.”

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's weight-hedged, Dutch-type reading from Gussenhoven 2000 (Roermond) and Peters 2006 (Hasselt): confirms that the tone contrast is anchored to the word-stressed syllable and that sentence accent works as in Standard Dutch, and adds that secondary stress on final syllables exists and can carry Accent 2 (Venlo). It is silent on the placement algorithm itself, which is why the catalog's existing tag for this source ('read: silent on stress') is also defensible; the quotes here match the ones the catalog already holds for it.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Limburgish has a binary lexical tone-accent contrast (Accent 1 vs Accent 2) that is confined to the syllable bearing word stress (one locus per simplex word, one per member in compounds); sentence accent is placed as in Standard Dutch/German. The survey presupposes a Dutch-type word-stress system and gives no placement algorithm; it shows that antepenult main stress with final secondary stress occurs (algebra, dominee) and, on p. 106, that in Venlo Accent 2 can also occur on a final syllable with secondary stress (olifant).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Present: words like algebra, dominee carry main stress on the antepenult and secondary stress on the final syllable (Maasbracht, after Hermans 1994, p. 105); in Venlo the tone contrast can appear on a final secondarily-stressed syllable too, so Accent 2 can occur twice in olifant (p. 106).
new_statements.exceptions: None on stress placement; the distributional restrictions discussed (pp. 105-106) concern which stressed rimes can carry the tone contrast (two sonorant moras in East Limburgish; Roermond/Maasbracht restrictions for /in, yn, un/ + nasal and nasal + voiceless obstruent).
new_statements.identity_note: Peters 2008 is about the dialect of Hasselt (Belgian Limburg, West Limburgish). Gussenhoven & Peters 2008 is a survey of the whole Limburgish tone area; its stress remarks are general (p. 90) or cite specific dialects: Maasbracht (Hermans 1994, p. 105) and Venlo (Gussenhoven & van der Vliet 1999, p. 106); it treats Hasselt and Roermond as the two worked grammars (sec. 3). The catalog entry itself covers Roermond (Gussenhoven 2000) and Hasselt (Peters 2006).

new_statements.quote: (p. 983, abstract) "The West-Limburgian dialect of Hasselt has a word accent distinction comparable to the distinction between accent 1 and accent 2 in Swedish and Norwegian. [...] The results suggest that Hasselt speakers, like speakers of the more eastern dialects of Venlo, Roermond, and Cologne, mark accent 2 by lexical tone, while accent 1 remains lexically toneless." (p. 986) "The word accent distinction is confined to word stressed syllables but not to primary word stress. Examples for words with accent 2 in a secondary stressed syllable are /'al2'tet2/ 'always' and /'øø2le'fant2/ 'elephant'. [...] In contrast to East-Limburgian dialects, the Hasselt dialect does not restrict the word accent contrast to syllables containing two or more sonorant moras."

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for limb1263 has an empty rule and there are no existing statements. This article adds that the Hasselt dialect is a tone-accent (pitch accent) system in which a lexical tone contrast rides on word-stressed syllables (primary or secondary), with the syllable as TBU; it does not supply a word-stress placement rule, so it neither confirms nor contradicts any placement. Compatible with the companion DBNL text already held by the project (Gussenhoven & Peters 2008, 'Het contrast is gelokaliseerd in de lettergreep met woordklemtoon').
new_statements.rule_in_words: Hasselt (West Limburgish) has a privative lexical tone-accent contrast of the Scandinavian accent-1/accent-2 type: accent 2 syllables carry a lexical L tone, accent 1 syllables are lexically toneless; the contrast is licensed only in syllables bearing word stress (primary or secondary) and, unlike Venlo/Roermond/Cologne, is not restricted to syllables with two sonorant moras (CVC syllables can bear accent 2); the TBU is the stressed syllable rather than the sonorant mora; one intonational pitch accent LH* docks on stressed syllables. The article presupposes Germanic-type word stress (marks it with ˈ and ˌ in transcriptions) but nowhere states a rule for where word stress falls.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary word stress exists and can host the tone-accent contrast (accent 2 on secondary-stressed syllables in 'always', 'elephant', p. 986); reduced schwa syllables 'do not count as a bearer of full word stress' (fn. 7, p. 1015). No placement rule for secondary stress is given.
new_statements.exceptions: fn. 5: no basis for distinguishing stressed accent-1 syllables from stressed syllables without accent (accent 1 = default/toneless); East Limburgish (Venlo, Roermond, Cologne) restricts the contrast to stressed syllables with at least two sonorant moras, Hasselt does not (Staelens 1989 vs Grootaers & Grauls 1930 disagree on CVC accent 2; Peters' data support accent 2 on CVC). In accent-2 words the focal peak is displaced to the last syllable before the next stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Peters 2008 describes the West-Limburgian dialect of Hasselt (Belgian Limburg; nine speakers aged 49-82), with systematic comparison to the East-Limburgian dialects of Venlo and Roermond and to Cologne; the catalog entry limb1263 bundles 'Roermond Dutch and the dialect of Hasselt', and the article covers the Hasselt half directly and Roermond only by comparison (Roermond: lexical H on the second sonorant mora of the stressed syllable, contrast restricted to bimoraic stressed syllables).

tone_statements.citation: Goossens, Jan. 2017. De oorsprong van de Rijnlands-Limburgse tweetonigheid: een analyse met bijzondere aandacht voor de korte klinkers voor obstruent. Handelingen van de Koninklijke Commissie voor Toponymie en Dialectologie 89: 129-185.
tone_statements.quote: De Rijnlands-Limburgse tweetonigheid is dus tot stand gekomen doordat hier in een sonoriteitsscala, een gegeven dat in principe in iedere taal van de wereld voorkomt, op een bepaald punt een breuk is ontstaan, die tot een groepering in twee polariserende betoningen heeft geleid.
tone_statements.translation: The Rhenish-Limburgian bitonality thus came about because here, in a sonority scale, something that in principle occurs in every language of the world, a break arose at a certain point, which led to a grouping into two polarising accentuations.
tone_statements.locator: p. 176 (section 5 conclusion); research history pp. 129-140; Haspengouw pp. 148-157
tone_statements.summary: Binary Franconian tone accent (stoottoon/sleeptoon) on stressed syllables incl. short vowel + obstruent rhymes in Genk; partial neutralisation and local loss in Haspengouw/Maastricht area.

tone_statements.citation: Fournier, Rachel, Jo Verhoeven, Marc Swerts & Carlos Gussenhoven. 2006. Perceiving word prosodic contrasts as a function of sentence prosody in two Dutch Limburgian dialects. Journal of Phonetics 34(1): 29-48.
tone_statements.quote: In these dialects, number can be marked segmentally or prosodically. The Roermond dialect, but not theWeert dialect, appears to neutralize the prosodic distinction outside the focus constituent in IP-internal syllables. We explain this difference between the dialects on the basis of the specific prosodic marking used, duration in the Weert dialect and F0 in the Roermond dialect.
tone_statements.summary: Roermond: F0-based binary tone accent with positional neutralisation; Weert: durational reflex of the former tone contrast.

tone_statements.citation: Hermans, Ben & Marc van Oostendorp. 1999. Synchrone beperkingen op de Sittardse diftongering. Taal en Tongval 51: 166-186.
tone_statements.quote: This article deals with the interaction between diphtongisation and tone structure in Sittard Dutch. Sittard, like other Limburg Dutch dialects, distinguishes between a so-called dragging (hlh) tone and a falling (hl) tone contour on the syllable that carries primary stress in a word. In Sittard Dutch certain mid vowels get diphthongized in a stressed position.
tone_statements.locator: p. 166, English 'Summary' at the head of the article (DBNL HTML); body statement p. ~174 sec. 3 'Lange middenklinkers die een sleeptoon dragen diftongeren nooit.'
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Binary lexical tone-accent contrast (Accent 1 valtoon HL vs Accent 2 sleeptoon) on the primary-stressed syllable; in Sittard the falling accent triggers diphthongization of long mid vowels.

tone_statements.citation: Goossens, J. 1956. Stoottoon en diftongering van Wgm. î en û in Limburg. Taal en Tongval 8: 99-112.
tone_statements.quote: Er is nog een derde geval: op een aantal plaatsen worden wgm. î en û voor een medeklinker gediftongeerd indien hun reflex stoottonig is (verscherping vertoont).
tone_statements.translation: There is a third case: in a number of places WGmc. long i and long u before a consonant are diphthongised if their reflex carries push tone (shows sharpening).
tone_statements.summary: Binary tone accent presupposed; stoottoon triggers diphthongisation of high long vowels.

tone_statements.citation: Stevens, A. 1955. Intonatieproblemen in en om West-Limburg. Taal en Tongval 7: 135-142.
tone_statements.quote: Een zaak is echter zeker: de fonologische oppositie tussen sleep- en stoottoon is in het betrokken gebied vóór okklusieven en vóór bepaalde kategorieën van spiranten opgeheven wanneer de voorafgaande klank een korte vokaal is.
tone_statements.translation: One thing is certain, however: in the area concerned the phonological opposition between dragging tone and push tone is suspended before occlusives and before certain categories of spirants when the preceding sound is a short vowel.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 141-142 (end of section I.B); also pp. 137-138
tone_statements.summary: Binary tone accent (sleeptoon vs stoottoon), neutralised on short vowel + voiceless obstruent rhymes in East Haspengouw.

tone_statements.citation: Verstegen, V. 1946. Bijdrage tot de tonologie van de Oostlimburgse dialecten. Handelingen van de Koninklijke Commissie voor Toponymie en Dialectologie 20: 99-108.
tone_statements.quote: Voldoende is bekend dat er twee accenten of tonen bestaan die we zullen benoemen met de bij ons best bekende en gemakkelijkste benamingen van sleeptoon en stoottoon. Met een van beide accenten nu wordt elke beklemtoonde lettergreep uitgespröken en die intonatie is dan ook phonologisch relevant. Dit is het geval in onze Zuidnederlandse Limburgse dialecten; mogelijk is dit niet overal zo.
tone_statements.translation: It is sufficiently well known that there are two accents or tones, which we shall call by the names best known and easiest for us, sleeptoon (dragging tone) and stoottoon (push tone). Every stressed syllable is pronounced with one of these two accents, and that intonation is accordingly phonologically relevant. This is the case in our South-Netherlandic Limburgish dialects; possibly it is not so everywhere.
tone_statements.summary: Binary lexical tone accent (sleeptoon/stoottoon) on the stressed syllable, with morphological (number) function and vowel-quality interaction.

tone_statements.citation: Dols, Willy. 1941. Een phonologisch probleem der Limburgsche dialecten. Onze Taaltuin 9: 193-211.
tone_statements.quote: We kunnen nu vragen: heeft in de L.D. èlke beklemtoonde lettergreep een phonologisch relevante intonatie? Het antwoord luidt neen! Want alleen lettergrepen met een langen syllabedrager laten de correlatieve tegenstelling sleeptoon-valtoon toe, lettergrepen met een korten syllabedrager sluiten die uit.
tone_statements.translation: We may now ask: does every stressed syllable in the Limburgish dialects have a phonologically relevant intonation? The answer is no! For only syllables with a long syllable nucleus admit the correlative opposition dragging tone vs falling tone; syllables with a short nucleus exclude it.
tone_statements.summary: Binary lexical tone accent restricted to stressed syllables with two sonorant moras (Sittard).

tone.quote: This article deals with the interaction between diphtongisation and tone structure in Sittard Dutch. Sittard, like other Limburg Dutch dialects, distinguishes between a so-called dragging (hlh) tone and a falling (hl) tone contour on the syllable that carries primary stress in a word. In Sittard Dutch certain mid vowels get diphthongized in a stressed position.

sources.quote: Voldoende is bekend dat er twee accenten of tonen bestaan die we zullen benoemen met de bij ons best bekende en gemakkelijkste benamingen van sleeptoon en stoottoon. Met een van beide accenten nu wordt elke beklemtoonde lettergreep uitgespröken en die intonatie is dan ook phonologisch relevant. Dit is het geval in onze Zuidnederlandse Limburgse dialecten; mogelijk is dit niet overal zo.
sources.note: States that every stressed syllable in these South-Netherlandic Limburgish dialects carries one of two phonologically relevant tones (sleeptoon vs stoottoon), contra Dols's restriction to long syllable nuclei; notes the pitch direction differs by place (Tongeren sleeptoon rising, stoottoon falling; sometimes the reverse in Maasland dialects); tone alone marks sg/pl in some nouns; main topic: tone alternation correlates with vowel-quality alternation (stoottoon opener, sleeptoon closer vowels) in Mechelen-aan-de-Maas.

tone.translation: It is sufficiently well known that there are two accents or tones, which we shall call by the names best known and easiest for us, sleeptoon (dragging tone) and stoottoon (push tone). Every stressed syllable is pronounced with one of these two accents, and that intonation is accordingly phonologically relevant. This is the case in our South-Netherlandic Limburgish dialects; possibly it is not so everywhere.

sources.note: Prague-school analysis of the Limburgish 'polytonie' (toonverloopcorrelatie): the stressed syllable carries a word-distinguishing intonation, sleeptoon vs valtoon (e.g. bal 'ball to play with' vs bal 'dance'), but only syllables with a long nucleus (long vowels, diphthongs, short vowel + certain consonants) admit the opposition; syllables with a short nucleus exclude it; then discusses the interaction with the quantity/Silbenschnitt correlation after Trubetzkoy.
